findings.problem: The concise References name four loci that the concise never cites, quotes or relies on. They are carried over from the expansive study: Douay-Rheims Ps 145:2 ('Put not your trust in princes', which only the expansive's Cyrus-and-Caesar reading cites through Aquinas); Augustine, En. in Ps. 95.5 ('All nations then had devils for their gods', expansive only; the concise cites 95.2, 95.3 and 95.8-9); Augustine, En. in Ps. 118 under Schin ('Did their King forbid His soldiers to pay...', expansive only); and Aquinas, Postilla super Psalmos 16 (the Gloss on the pupil, expansive only; the concise uses Postilla 32 alone). A search of all six concise components finds no use of any of them. The references-used preflight checks at the level of the work, not the locus, so it passes. The universal editorial standard requires the 'absence of unused references' before installation (guidance/editorial.md, pre-install list). The three-document profile forbids padding the short work with the full study's apparatus. No later stage of the run checks reference use at locus level.
findings.required_result: The concise References list only loci the concise actually uses. Remove '145:2' from the Douay-Rheims item, '5' and '118, under Schin' from the Augustine Enarrationes item, and '16 and' from the Postilla item. A locus may be kept only if the reviser cites it at the place in the concise prose that already relies on it, adding no new claim. Nothing else needs to change.

findings.problem: About eleven witness statements, several of them decisive, appear only in Latin. They include Aquinas's definition of the hypocrite, on which the third reading turns, his lesson against believing flatterers, and Jerome's and Aquinas's sentences on the counter-question. The expansive study renders each in English, and the concise apparatus itself says 'English glosses of Latin are the editor's'. A reader without Latin recovers the gist only from the summary sentences around them, such as 'mouth against heart'. To see exactly what the witness says, that reader has to open the long work, and the concise is meant to stand without it.
findings.required_result: Each listed Latin phrase carries a brief English rendering beside it, reusing the expansive study's own renderings where they exist, with no new claim. Where space is short, trim Latin rather than enlarge type or pad.

findings.location: src/claude/liturgy/roman-rite/postconciliar/roman-missal-third-edition-en-us-2011/propers/temporal/pc-s55-twenty-ninth-sunday-in-ordinary-time-year-a/sections/concise/90-apparatus.tex line 32, 'Relations among the elements' (PDF p. 10): 'the psalm responds to the first reading; the Alleluia verse greets the Gospel'; References, 'Liturgical books and Bibles'
findings.problem: The paragraph says 'The liturgical books state four relations' but sources only the first (Praenotanda 105-107). The expansive study cites General Instruction 61 for the psalm's response to the first reading and General Instruction 62 for the acclamation greeting the Gospel. The concise cites neither and does not list the General Instruction in its References, so its own reader cannot verify two of the four official relations on which the commentary's reading of the psalm and acclamation rests.
findings.required_result: Cite General Instruction 61 and 62 beside those two relations and add the United States General Instruction of the Roman Missal to the References, as the expansive study does, with no other change.

summary: Cold review of the concise study src/claude/liturgy/roman-rite/postconciliar/roman-missal-third-edition-en-us-2011/propers/temporal/pc-s55-twenty-ninth-sunday-in-ordinary-time-year-a/synthesis.tex and its six components (sealed bytes checked against REVIEW_INPUTS; all fifteen hashes match). I rebuilt it independently to a fixed point in my scratch area: 11 pages, aux settled from the first pass, no warnings or overfull boxes, 16 fonts embedded, PDF SHA-256 244e271358ae5d19d9ad68d0474dc1ff8a636b48f825c057e404044d81ebdb11, byte-identical to the author's retained proof. zref abspages: inventory and all four sense markers p1, chronology p2, themes p3-4, commentary p5; check-proper-components --phase artifacts --edition synthesis on my aux is valid. I read every page raster. From the concise prose alone, before opening the full study, I recovered the three answers: (1) 'the things that are God's' are the self that bears God's image (Augustine, with Ambrose's Christ who bears no image of Caesar, and Hilary reaching the whole self from its origin); its difficulty is that the saying never states the inference. (2) Caesar's claim is real because it lies inside the sovereignty of the Lord who took Cyrus's hand, and that same sovereignty bounds it (Chrysostom's render-not-give and his limit at godliness; Augustine's soldiers under Julian). Hilary and Ambrose ground the debt in possession, and the difficulty is that no Father joins Isaiah 45 to Matthew 22. (3) True words from a divided heart, with Christ's reading of that heart as the sign of his Godhead (Chrysostom, Hilary, Aquinas), against Jerome's rule of prudence. Pages 5-10 set these answers side by side in seven questions. They develop the reasoning and do not repeat the opening's conclusions. Disagreements survive without theatre, and every qualification I tested survived compression: Augustine's 'some', the Old Latin 'from the wood', Romans 13 and Acts 17 not read, the unsung contexts of Ps 16:8, Ps 32:16 and Mk 10:42-43, 'sincere' falling outside the acclamation's words, and the alternative Communion antiphons. A shingle comparison and a check of every concise quotation against the study's sections found no quotation or source-dependent claim absent from the accepted study. I checked the cited sources at their loci: Augustine (Enarrationes 4.8, 16.2, 16.8, 57.8, 95.2-3, 95.8-9, 115.13, 124.7-8; Tractatus 40.9 including 1 Jn 3:2, 41.2; De sermone II.20.70), Chrysostom (Hom. Matt. 6, 65.4, 70.1-2; Rom. 23; 1 Thess. 1; Phil. 8), Cyril, Justin, Bellarmine and Bede in their tracked texts; Ambrose IX.34-35 in the electronic Latin; Jerome on Matthew (PL 26 col. 163), Hilary 23.1-2 (PL 9 cols. 1044-1045) and Aquinas on Matthew (Venice pp. 283-284) on their page images; Drum's 'Psalms' line 303 for the prophetic-referent phrase. Page-2 lookup on the rendered table: Second Reading 1 Thes 1:1-5b leads to the last row, which dates the letter's composition ('Paul writes from Corinth (an ancient subscription says Athens) to the church at Thessalonica'; Disputed: A.D. 52; A.D. 53-54). That matches row-d67f41bffc530c4a and the study's appendix phrase. First Reading Is 45:1, 4-6 leads to two rows: Isaias's ministry, B.C. 740-701, and the NABRE placement of chs. 40-55 toward the end of the exile. The footnote says neither dates the oracle. Gospel Mt 22:15-21 leads to an event row (in the temple at Jerusalem; Date unresolved) and a composition row with six disputed alternatives. Communion antiphon A, Ps 32:18-19, appears in three labelled rows, including the Davidic attribution (Disputed: B.C. 1055-1015), which says 'The reign dates David, not the psalm'. Outcome: every appointed passage pairs with its occurrence, place and date without crossing a paragraph. Shared rows name every use, no composite element is paired with unrelated dates, and all twelve rows and place phrases are identical to the reviewed expansive appendix. Limits: I did not re-read Jerome on Isaiah (PL 24), Aquinas on Isaiah (Parma), the Corpus Thomisticum texts or the chronology corpus beyond its generated annotations; for these I relied on the study's identical wording and its passed review. Verdict CHANGES_REQUIRED on one blocking finding: the References list four loci the concise does not use. Two advisories ask for English glosses of decisive Latin and sources for two official relations. Independence: I did not open the GPT leaf, its outputs or its production reviews, and no search I ran printed a line from them.
